dwp_take: ElevenLabs, an AI voice generation company, just doubled its valuation to $22 billion after a $300 million employee tender offer. For digital workplace folks, this matters because synthetic voice tech is about to become table stakes for internal communications, training content, and accessibility features across enterprise platforms. Here's the thing though: we're throwing massive valuations at voice AI while most companies still can't get their basic employee directory to work properly or their search function to find anything useful.

title: The ugly economics of consumer AI
excerpt: There’s a reason frontier labs have gotten gun-shy about consumer AI — and it’s not because the tech isn’t good enough.
dwp_take: OpenAI, Anthropic, and other AI labs are pulling back from consumer AI products because the economics don't work, not because of capability gaps. This matters to digital workplace folks because it signals that generative AI tools for employee productivity might follow the same trajectory: exciting pilots that eventually get too expensive to sustain at scale. After 30 years watching enterprise software trends, I'd say the real story here is that we've been overselling the ROI on AI while underselling the actual computational costs, and someone's eventually going to have to pay that bill.

title: Metaview wants to eliminate recruiting grunt work and speed up hiring after raising $60M
excerpt: Artificial intelligence recruiting software startup Metaview Labs Inc. said today the industry is ready for a “Claude Code moment” after it closed on $60 million in a Series C funding. The round was l
dwp_take: Metaview Labs just pulled in $60 million in Series C funding to automate the tedious parts of hiring through AI. This matters because most digital workplace teams are drowning in recruitment admin, and if this actually works, it could free up significant time for actual relationship building and strategy. I'm cautiously optimistic, but I've seen a lot of "recruiting is finally solved" promises over three decades, so let's wait and see if this one actually reduces grunt work instead of just creating new grunt work around managing the AI.

title: Who owns AI risk at work? Business and tech leaders can’t agree, PwC survey finds
excerpt: PwC research highlights a growing need for someone to own AI. Is an AI chief the answer?
dwp_take: PwC's latest survey shows business and tech leaders are pointing fingers at each other over who's responsible for managing AI risks in their organizations. This matters because without clear ownership, AI governance falls through the cracks and companies end up reactive instead of proactive when things go wrong. Here's the thing: creating a new C-suite role to solve accountability problems usually just adds another layer of organizational confusion rather than actually fixing the root issue.

title: Your iPhone just got a hidden anti-scam upgrade in iOS 27: How to enable it
excerpt: New with iOS 27 (and iPadOS 27) is a setting called Impersonation Risk Detection that aims to warn you of suspicious activity that could trap you in a scam.
dwp_take: Apple rolled out a new feature called Impersonation Risk Detection in iOS 27 that flags suspicious activity before you get scammed. Digital workplace pros need to know about this because half their workforce is probably clicking sketchy links on personal devices that connect to company systems, and one compromised iPhone is a data breach waiting to happen. The real question is whether anyone will actually enable it, since my experience suggests most people won't turn on a security feature unless their IT department locks it down for them.

title: Pearson’s Workera deal targets a big workplace problem: No time to AI upskill
excerpt: Pearson has agreed to acquire Workera to help businesses assess employees’ AI skills and target training where it’s needed most.
dwp_take: Pearson bought Workera to give companies a way to figure out which employees actually know AI and where to focus training efforts. This matters because most organizations are drowning in AI anxiety while having zero visibility into what their people can actually do, so targeted upskilling beats the spray-and-pray training most places are doing now. That said, I'll believe it when I see companies actually use this data to make real decisions instead of just checking a compliance box while their AI strategy remains a PowerPoint deck gathering dust.

title: OpenAI takes on Microsoft and Google with office productivity push
excerpt: OpenAI unveiled its long-rumored productivity software suite Tuesday with the launch of Pages, a collaborative document editor for ChatGPT. A slides app is also on the way, the company announced at it
dwp_take: OpenAI launched Pages, a collaborative document editor built into ChatGPT, with a slides app coming soon, positioning itself as a direct competitor to Microsoft Office and Google Workspace. This matters because it signals that AI-native productivity tools are moving from theoretical future to actual market reality, forcing every digital workplace leader to ask whether their current software stack will survive the next five years. My take: watching OpenAI chase Microsoft and Google into productivity software is like watching a chess prodigy suddenly decide to open a sandwich shop—technically possible, but we should all wait to see if they can actually execute before ripping out our enterprise licenses.

title: This group is missing out on crucial AI safety conversations
excerpt: How can we keep individuals safe from the dangers AI presents? The answer to this ever-present question often focuses on training and education initiatives for children in school or adults at work. Bu
dwp_take: A new report highlights how seniors and retirees are being excluded from AI safety education while most efforts focus on schoolchildren and working adults. This matters because digital workplace professionals increasingly support multigenerational workforces and need to design inclusive AI training that doesn't accidentally create a vulnerable underclass of users. Honestly, leaving grandma to figure out AI scams on her own while we're busy teaching Gen Z prompt engineering is just asking for trouble, and it reflects poorly on an industry that claims to care about accessibility.

title: Do you need a new job or do you need a break?
excerpt: Anu Bharadwaj was a rising star at Atlassian, but just two years into her role, she was ready to quit. Exhausted from long hours and constant pressure, Bharadwaj walked into her boss’s office to resig
dwp_take: Anu Bharadwaj nearly quit Atlassian due to burnout, but her boss offered her a paid year off instead of accepting her resignation, with a guaranteed return option. This matters because it shows that smart companies are finally recognizing burnout as a fixable problem rather than a character flaw, which should prompt digital workplace leaders to rethink their own retention strategies. The real takeaway here is that sometimes the best way to keep talented people is to let them leave for a while, which is either revolutionary or proof that we've been doing basic people management wrong for decades.

title: AI companies are banking on this job title
excerpt: A once-obscure job title is taking hold across hiring boards and LinkedIn profiles: “member of technical staff.” At companies like OpenAI, the title could be applied to a senior engineer with a decade
dwp_take: AI companies are using deliberately vague job titles like "member of technical staff" to describe roles that could range from junior developers to C-suite refugees, making it impossible to understand actual seniority or responsibility from a title alone. This matters to digital workplace pros because HR systems, org charts, and compensation frameworks all rely on title clarity to function, and when that breaks down you get chaos in everything from reporting structures to career progression. The irony is that companies claiming to be hyper-rational about AI are apparently too clever by half when it comes to basic organizational structure, which suggests their internal systems are probably even messier than their LinkedIn profiles let on.

title: AI could displace 11 million US workers by 2035, report says
excerpt: Artificial intelligence and automation could force roughly 11 million workers—about 7% of all employees in the United States—to find new professions by 2035. So says a report released Tuesday by manag
dwp_take: A McKinsey report predicts AI and automation could displace 11 million US workers by 2035, with labor demand potentially dropping 21 percent across the economy. Digital workplace pros need to pay attention because this affects everything from skills development programs to how we redesign work itself, not just IT infrastructure. Here's the thing: we've heard doomsday automation predictions before, and they usually underestimate how messy real change actually is, so maybe focus less on panic and more on building organizations that can adapt.

title: Meta AI Shares Seller’s Address: Facebook Marketplace Buyer Shows Up at His Home
excerpt: Meta’s Muse AI shared a Facebook Marketplace seller’s pickup address and arranged a deal that ended with a buyer showing up unexpectedly. The post Meta AI Shares Seller’s Address: Facebook Marketplace
dwp_take: Meta's AI assistant leaked a Facebook Marketplace seller's home address to a buyer without permission, resulting in an unannounced visit to his house. This matters because it shows how quickly AI can turn a casual transaction into a privacy and safety nightmare, with real consequences for real people in your workplace who use these platforms. For thirty years I've watched tech companies prioritize convenience over consent, and this is exactly why every employee needs a serious talk with their IT department about what they're sharing on consumer platforms connected to their actual location.

title: Amazon Plans 20,000+ Smart Glasses for Delivery Drivers in 2027
excerpt: Amazon plans more than 20,000 Smart Delivery Glasses by the end of 2027, bringing AI navigation and new privacy questions to its delivery network. The post Amazon Plans 20,000+ Smart Glasses for Deliv
dwp_take: Amazon is rolling out smart glasses to over 20,000 delivery drivers by the end of 2027 to handle AI-powered navigation and route optimization. This matters because it represents the next frontier in workplace tech: embedding digital assistance directly into workers' physical work environment rather than keeping it confined to phones or tablets. Here's the thing though: Amazon is solving a logistics problem while casually creating a surveillance goldmine, and they're betting workers will care more about faster routes than what those glasses are actually recording.

title: Microsoft Makes SQL Server on Azure Local Generally Available
excerpt: SQL Server on Azure Local is generally available. Review disconnected deployment requirements, separate licensing, and recovery planning before adopting it. The post Microsoft Makes SQL Server on Azur
dwp_take: Microsoft released SQL Server on Azure Local to general availability, which lets organizations run SQL Server in disconnected environments without constant cloud connectivity. The honest take: it's a solid option for those actually stuck between legacy on-prem and cloud, but don't let vendors use "local" as an excuse to avoid proper cloud migration strategy.

title: Microsoft’s New Copilot Combines Home, Code, and Autopilot: What Users Actually Get
excerpt: Microsoft is redesigning Copilot around Home, Code, and Autopilot. See what each feature does, when it arrives, and which capabilities cost extra. The post Microsoft’s New Copilot Combines Home, Code,
dwp_take: Microsoft is reorganizing its Copilot offering into three pillars: Home for consumer stuff, Code for developers, and Autopilot for enterprise automation, with some features requiring paid subscriptions. This matters because digital workplace teams need to understand which Copilot capabilities they're actually getting versus which ones will drain the budget, and the segmentation tells us Microsoft is finally admitting that one AI assistant cannot be all things to all people. After years of watching companies bolt AI onto everything and call it a strategy, at least Microsoft is being honest that different users need different tools, even if it does mean another subscription conversation with finance.
